extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys and practitioners involved in EPO opposition and appeal proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when and how lack of clarity (Article 84 EPC) may be examined following amendments made during EPO opposition and opposition-appeal proceedings, based on Enlarged Board decision G 3/14. Focuses on incorporation of dependent-claim features into independent claims and related clarity/added-matter consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: When Article 84 may be examined in opposition proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with Article 84 EPC may be examined only when, and to the extent that, the amendment introduces non-compliance with Article 84 EPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Enlarged Board ruled (G 3/14) that the 'conventional' approach applies: claims may be examined for Article 84 only to the extent the amendment itself gives rise to a lack of clarity. The rationale includes that Article 84 is not a ground of opposition and amendment should not open the door to broad re-examination of clarity by third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between Article 84 and opposition grounds (Article 100) / Article 101(3) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of compliance with Article 84 EPC may not be used as a ground of opposition (Article 100 EPC); however where an amendment is made in opposition or appeal proceedings the patent must 'meet the requirements of the EPC' (Article 101(3) EPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Article 84 is not a ground of opposition, when claims are amended during opposition the requirement of clarity must nonetheless be considered to the extent the amendment creates non-compliance. This point is consistent with G 9/91 regarding requirements applying to maintained amended patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction of a complete dependent claim into an independent claim
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment consisting of striking out the original independent claim and then writing out the previous dependent claim in full (i.e. introduction of the features of a complete dependent claim) should not be subject to any examination for clarity under Article 84 EPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Enlarged Board concluded that such amendments are effectively drafting the dependent claim in independent form and therefore do not open Article 84 scrutiny in opposition proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction of elements from a dependent claim that are simple alternatives or deletion of optional features
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments based on an embodiment expressed as an alternative in a dependent claim, or involving deletion of wording from a dependent claim thereby narrowing its scope, or involving the deletion of optional features, are to be treated the same as introduction of a complete dependent claim and are not open to Article 84 examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if a dependent claim specifies 'substantially concave or convex, optionally having a radius of curvature of at least 10 mm', amending to specify a 'substantially concave surface' (a simple alternative together with deletion of an optional feature) will avoid Article 84 scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments that disconnect previously linked features are examinable for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments which disconnect features from other features to which they were previously linked in a dependent claim are open to examination under Article 84 EPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if a dependent claim specifies a 'substantially concave surface having a radius of curvature of at least 10 mm', amending to specify merely a 'substantially concave surface' (thus removing the radius-of-curvature link) may be examined for clarity. Such amendments may also give rise to added-subject-matter issues depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three strands of case law on clarity examination (contextual standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Case law developed three approaches: (1) the 'conventional' approach—clarity examined only to the extent it arises out of the amendment; (2) an extended 'arising out of' approach—where clarity problems concealed in dependent claims are highlighted by amendment; and (3) a diverging/wider approach—allowing broader examination of clarity after amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Enlarged Board analysed these strands and endorsed the 'conventional' approach (approach 1), rejecting the wider approaches. This decision provides authoritative guidance on which prior decisions are consistent or inconsistent with G 3/14.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical example guidance (surface / radius of curvature scenarios)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific examples illustrate when clarity can or cannot be examined: (a) claim 1 refers to a surface and claim 2 specifies 'substantially flat' → amending claim 1 to 'substantially flat surface' (introduction of the complete dependent claim feature) cannot be examined for clarity; (b) dependent claim listing alternatives including an optional radius → selecting one alternative and deleting an optional feature avoids scrutiny; (c) removing a radius limitation that was linked to the feature can attract clarity examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples show application of the rule to common drafting patterns and highlight where disconnection of linked features triggers Article 84 scrutiny. The discussion also notes potential overlap with added-subject-matter concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences when clarity cannot be raised during opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patentee seeks to rely on a feature from a dependent claim which is inherently unclear, even if lack of clarity cannot be raised as a ground, the EPO is likely to give that feature a broad meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broadly interpreted unclear feature may prevent establishing a useful distinction over the prior art. Decision T 1459/05 is cited as an example where the Board gave an unclear feature a broad meaning — the Enlarged Board cited that decision despite disagreeing with its overall approach to Article 84 examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy rationale limiting clarity scrutiny after amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendment should not open a door to allow third parties to scrutinise a patent thoroughly for compliance with all the requirements of the EPC; therefore clarity examination is limited to amendment-caused issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Enlarged Board acknowledged it is not optimal that patents may be granted with claims that do not comply with Article 84 EPC but emphasised the legislature's choice not to make Article 84 a ground of opposition. Practically, amendments arise in a high proportion of oppositions (~70%), so the limitation prevents broad re-litigation of clarity on many amended patents.
